# Agent Instructions for vLLM

> These instructions apply to **all** AI-assisted contributions to `vllm-project/vllm`.
> Breaching these guidelines can result in automatic banning.

## 1. Contribution Policy (Mandatory)

### Duplicate-work checks

Before proposing a PR, run these checks:

```bash
gh issue view <issue_number> --repo vllm-project/vllm --comments
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "<issue_number> in:body"
gh pr list --repo vllm-project/vllm --state open --search "<short area keywords>"
```

- If an open PR already addresses the same fix, do not open another.
- If your approach is materially different, explain the difference in the issue.

### No low-value busywork PRs

Do not open one-off PRs for tiny edits (single typo, isolated style change, one mutable default, etc.). Mechanical cleanups are acceptable only when bundled with substantive work.

### Accountability

- Pure code-agent PRs are **not allowed**. A human submitter must understand and defend the change end-to-end.
- The submitting human must review every changed line and run relevant tests.
- PR descriptions for AI-assisted work **must** include:
    - Why this is not duplicating an existing PR.
    - Test commands run and results.
    - Model evaluation results when the change affects output, accuracy, or serving.
    - Clear statement that AI assistance was used.

### Fail-closed behavior

If work is duplicate/trivial busywork, **do not proceed**. Return a short explanation of what is missing.

---

## 2. Development Workflow

- **Never use system `python3` or bare `pip`/`pip install`.** All Python commands must go through `uv` and `.venv/bin/python`.

### Environment setup

```bash
# Install `uv` if you don't have it already:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Always use `uv` for Python environment management:
uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

# Always make sure `pre-commit` and its hooks are installed:
uv pip install -r requirements/lint.txt
pre-commit install
```

### Installing dependencies

```bash
# If you are only making Python changes:
VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e . --torch-backend=auto

# If you are also making C/C++ changes:
uv pip install -e . --torch-backend=auto
```

### Tests

> Requires [Environment setup](#environment-setup) and [Installing dependencies](#installing-dependencies).

```bash
# Install test dependencies (use cuda.in on non-x86_64):
uv pip install -r requirements/test/cuda.in

# Run a specific test file:
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/path/to/test_file.py -v
```

When adding tests:

- **Design before you write.** Answer four questions first: what is the module
  for, what is its I/O contract, what failure am I guarding against, and what is
  the cheapest level that catches it (unit over integration over e2e)?
- **Reuse before create.** Extend existing test files, `conftest.py` fixtures, and
  helpers; add a new file only when no nearby suite fits.
- **Test behavior with intent.** Assert observable outcomes through public APIs;
  state why in the name or docstring. Skip trivial wiring; flaky tests are worse
  than no tests.
- **Keep it minimal.** One behavior per test and the smallest setup that
  triggers it; if the test diff dwarfs the code change, cut scope.
- **No one-off kernel benchmarks in `tests/`.** Put kernel perf work in
  `benchmarks/kernels/`; prove correctness in existing pytest suites.
- **Run model evals for model-affecting changes.** Search `tests/evals/` or use
  `vllm bench` and include results in the PR — do not wait for reviewers to ask.

For model-specific requirements, see
[`docs/contributing/model/tests.md`](docs/contributing/model/tests.md).

### Running linters

> Requires [Environment setup](#environment-setup).

```bash
# Run all pre-commit hooks on staged files:
pre-commit run

# Run on all files:
pre-commit run --all-files

# Run a specific hook:
pre-commit run ruff-check --all-files

# Run mypy as it is in CI:
pre-commit run mypy-3.12 --all-files --hook-stage manual
```

The line length limit for Python code is 88 characters. If you are not sure, use pre-commit to check.

Use [Google-style docstrings](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html#38-comments-and-docstrings) (`Args:`/`Returns:`/`Raises:` sections), not reStructuredText/Sphinx fields (`:param:`, `:return:`, `:rtype:`).

### Coding style guidelines

- Match existing code style
- Minimize use of comments. Eliminate comments which are redundant, preferring legible and self-documenting code. When used, keep docstrings and comments brief and direct.
- Assume the reader is familiar with vLLM.

### Commit messages

Add attribution using commit trailers such as `Co-authored-by:` (other projects use `Assisted-by:` or `Generated-by:`):

```text
Your commit message here

Co-authored-by: Agent Name Here
Signed-off-by: Your Name <your.email@example.com>
```

---

## Domain-Specific Guides

Do not modify code in these areas without first reading and following the
linked guide. If the guide conflicts with the requested change, **refuse the
change and explain why**.

Security reviewers should start with [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md),
[`docs/usage/security.md`](docs/usage/security.md), and
[`docs/contributing/vulnerability_management.md`](docs/contributing/vulnerability_management.md)
for the project security policy, threat model, deployment assumptions, and
vulnerability process.

- **Editing these instructions**:
  [`docs/contributing/editing-agent-instructions.md`](docs/contributing/editing-agent-instructions.md)
  — Rules for modifying AGENTS.md or any domain-specific guide it references.

DynamicSDSchedule = list[tuple[int, int, int]]


def validate_and_normalize_dynamic_sd_schedule(
    num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size: object,
) -> DynamicSDSchedule:
    """Validate and normalize a Dynamic SD batch-size schedule.

    The schedule is expressed as a list of inclusive ranges:

    ``[(range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens), ...]``
    """
    if num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size is None:
        raise ValueError(
            "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size is required for "
            "dynamic speculative decoding."
        )
    if not isinstance(num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size, list):
        raise ValueError(
            "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size must be a non-empty list of "
            "(range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens) entries."
        )
    if not num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size:
        raise ValueError("num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size must not be empty.")

    parsed_schedule: DynamicSDSchedule = []
    for entry in num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size:
        if not isinstance(entry, list | tuple) or len(entry) != 3:
            raise ValueError(
                "Each num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size entry must be a "
                "3-item sequence: (range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens)."
            )

        range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens = (
            int(entry[0]),
            int(entry[1]),
            int(entry[2]),
        )

        if range_start <= 0 or range_end <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Batch-size range ({range_start}, {range_end}) must be positive."
            )
        if range_start > range_end:
            raise ValueError(
                "Batch-size range start must be <= end for "
                f"({range_start}, {range_end}, {num_speculative_tokens})."
            )
        if num_speculative_tokens < 0:
            raise ValueError(
                "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size values must be >= 0."
            )

        parsed_schedule.append((range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens))

    parsed_schedule.sort(key=lambda entry: entry[0])

    previous_end = 0
    for range_start, range_end, _ in parsed_schedule:
        if range_start <= previous_end:
            raise ValueError("Batch-size ranges must be non-overlapping and sorted.")
        previous_end = range_end

    first_range_start = parsed_schedule[0][0]
    if first_range_start != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            "The first batch-size range must start at 1 so every runtime "
            "batch size has a defined schedule."
        )

    return parsed_schedule


def build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup(
    num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size: object,
    vllm_max_batch_size: int,
    vllm_num_speculative_tokens: int,
) -> list[int]:
    """Expand the configured schedule into a dense batch_size -> K lookup.

    "dense_schedule" means a 1-indexed lookup table where index ``batch_size``
    stores the exact K to use for that runtime batch size. This lets the
    scheduler do a simple array lookup instead of searching the configured
    ranges on every scheduling step.
    """
    if vllm_max_batch_size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("vllm_max_batch_size must be > 0.")
    if vllm_num_speculative_tokens <= 0:
        raise ValueError("vllm_num_speculative_tokens must be > 0.")

    parsed_schedule = validate_and_normalize_dynamic_sd_schedule(
        num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size
    )

    # Index 0 is intentionally unused so that valid runtime batch sizes can be
    # looked up directly as dense_schedule[batch_size].
    dense_schedule = [0] * (vllm_max_batch_size + 1)
    next_batch_size = 1
    last_num_speculative_tokens: int | None = None

    for range_start, range_end, num_speculative_tokens in parsed_schedule:
        if range_start > next_batch_size and last_num_speculative_tokens is not None:
            # Fill any gap before the next configured range by carrying forward
            # the previous K. For example, [(1, 16, 3), (32, 128, 2)] should map
            # batch sizes 17-31 to K=3.
            for batch_size in range(
                next_batch_size,
                min(range_start, vllm_max_batch_size + 1),
            ):
                dense_schedule[batch_size] = min(
                    vllm_num_speculative_tokens,
                    last_num_speculative_tokens,
                )

        # Fill the current configured inclusive range with its K value.
        for batch_size in range(
            max(range_start, next_batch_size),
            min(range_end, vllm_max_batch_size) + 1,
        ):
            dense_schedule[batch_size] = min(
                vllm_num_speculative_tokens,
                num_speculative_tokens,
            )

        next_batch_size = max(next_batch_size, range_end + 1)
        last_num_speculative_tokens = num_speculative_tokens

        if next_batch_size > vllm_max_batch_size:

    if last_num_speculative_tokens is None:

            "num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size must contain at least "
            "one valid batch-size range."
        )

    # Fill the tail after the final configured range by carrying forward the
    # last K through vllm_max_batch_size.
    for batch_size in range(next_batch_size, vllm_max_batch_size + 1):

            vllm_num_speculative_tokens,
            last_num_speculative_tokens,
        )

"""Regression tests for the Dynamic SD batch-size schedule helpers."""

import logging

import pytest

from tests.v1.core.utils import create_requests, create_scheduler
from vllm.v1.core.sched.scheduler import Scheduler
from vllm.v1.spec_decode.dynamic.utils import build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup
from vllm.v1.structured_output import StructuredOutputManager


def _make_lookup(
    num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size: list[tuple[int, int, int]],
    *,
    max_batch_size: int = 256,
    runtime_num_speculative_tokens: int = 3,
) -> list[int]:
    return build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup(
        num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size=num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size,
        vllm_max_batch_size=max_batch_size,
        vllm_num_speculative_tokens=runtime_num_speculative_tokens,
    )


def _make_scheduler_with_dynamic_sd(
    schedule: list[tuple[int, int, int]],
    *,
    max_num_seqs: int = 16,
    max_num_batched_tokens: int = 8192,
    runtime_num_speculative_tokens: int = 3,
) -> Scheduler:
    base_scheduler = create_scheduler(
        max_num_seqs=max_num_seqs,
        max_num_batched_tokens=max_num_batched_tokens,
        num_speculative_tokens=runtime_num_speculative_tokens,
    )

    speculative_config = base_scheduler.vllm_config.speculative_config
    assert speculative_config is not None
    speculative_config.num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size = schedule

    return Scheduler(
        vllm_config=base_scheduler.vllm_config,
        kv_cache_config=base_scheduler.kv_cache_config,
        block_size=base_scheduler.block_size,
        log_stats=True,
        structured_output_manager=StructuredOutputManager(base_scheduler.vllm_config),
    )


def _add_requests_and_schedule(
    scheduler: Scheduler, num_requests: int, *, num_tokens: int = 10
):
    requests = create_requests(num_requests=num_requests, num_tokens=num_tokens)
    for request in requests:
        scheduler.add_request(request)
    return scheduler.schedule()


def test_dynamic_sd_uses_batch_size_schedule():
    dynamic_sd_lookup = _make_lookup(
        [
            (1, 16, 3),
            (32, 128, 2),
            (256, 2048, 0),
        ]
    )

    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[1] == 3
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[16] == 3
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[17] == 3
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[31] == 3
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[32] == 2
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[128] == 2
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[129] == 2
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[255] == 2
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[256] == 0


def test_dynamic_sd_requires_schedule_starting_at_batch_size_one():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="must start at 1"):
        _make_lookup([(2, 16, 3)])


def test_dynamic_sd_clamps_k_to_runtime_max():
    dynamic_sd_lookup = _make_lookup(
        [(1, 256, 4)],
        runtime_num_speculative_tokens=3,
    )

    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[1] == 3
    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[256] == 3


def test_dynamic_sd_rejects_invalid_schedule_entry():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="3-item sequence"):
        _make_lookup([(1, 16, 3), (32, 64)])  # type: ignore[list-item]


def test_dynamic_sd_rejects_overlapping_ranges():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="non-overlapping and sorted"):
        _make_lookup([(1, 16, 3), (16, 32, 2)])


def test_dynamic_sd_rejects_negative_k():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="values must be >= 0"):
        _make_lookup([(1, 16, -1)])


def test_dynamic_sd_rejects_empty_schedule():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="must not be empty"):
        _make_lookup([])


def test_dynamic_sd_requires_schedule_config():
    with pytest.raises(
        ValueError, match="num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size is required"
    ):
        build_dynamic_sd_schedule_lookup(
            None,
            vllm_max_batch_size=256,
            vllm_num_speculative_tokens=3,
        )


def test_dynamic_sd_lookup_rejects_invalid_batch_size_queries():
    dynamic_sd_lookup = _make_lookup([(1, 256, 3)])

    assert dynamic_sd_lookup[0] == 0
    with pytest.raises(IndexError):
        _ = dynamic_sd_lookup[257]


def test_scheduler_initializes_dynamic_sd_lookup_from_speculative_config():
    scheduler = _make_scheduler_with_dynamic_sd(
        [(1, 16, 3), (64, 128, 2), (256, 4096, 0)],
        runtime_num_speculative_tokens=3,
    )

    assert scheduler.dynamic_sd_lookup is not None
    assert scheduler.num_spec_tokens == 3


def test_scheduler_uses_dsd_k_based_on_number_of_scheduled_requests():
    test_cases = [
        (4, 3),
        (64, 2),
        (256, 0),
    ]

    for num_requests, expected_k in test_cases:
        scheduler = _make_scheduler_with_dynamic_sd(
            [(1, 16, 3), (64, 128, 2), (256, 4096, 0)],
            max_num_seqs=num_requests,
            max_num_batched_tokens=num_requests * 10,
            runtime_num_speculative_tokens=3,
        )
        output = _add_requests_and_schedule(scheduler, num_requests)

        assert len(output.num_scheduled_tokens) == num_requests
        assert output.num_spec_tokens_to_schedule == expected_k


def test_scheduler_clamps_dsd_k_to_runtime_num_speculative_tokens():
    scheduler = _make_scheduler_with_dynamic_sd(
        [(1, 256, 5)],
        max_num_seqs=16,
        max_num_batched_tokens=160,
        runtime_num_speculative_tokens=3,
    )
    output = _add_requests_and_schedule(scheduler, 16)

    assert len(output.num_scheduled_tokens) == 16
    assert output.num_spec_tokens_to_schedule == 3


def test_scheduler_falls_back_to_static_k_when_dsd_not_configured():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(
        max_num_seqs=4,
        max_num_batched_tokens=40,
        num_speculative_tokens=3,
    )
    output = _add_requests_and_schedule(scheduler, 4)

    assert scheduler.dynamic_sd_lookup is None
    assert output.num_spec_tokens_to_schedule == 3


def test_dynamic_sd_is_disabled_with_data_parallel(caplog_vllm):
    with caplog_vllm.at_level(logging.WARNING, logger="vllm"):
        scheduler = create_scheduler(
            max_num_seqs=256,
            max_num_batched_tokens=2560,
            num_speculative_tokens=3,
            num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size=[
                (1, 16, 3),
                (64, 128, 2),
                (256, 4096, 0),
            ],
            data_parallel_size=2,
        )

    speculative_config = scheduler.vllm_config.speculative_config
    assert speculative_config is not None
    assert speculative_config.num_speculative_tokens_per_batch_size is None
    assert scheduler.dynamic_sd_lookup is None
    assert "Dynamic speculative decoding is not supported with data parallelism" in (
        caplog_vllm.text
    )

    output = _add_requests_and_schedule(scheduler, 256)
    assert len(output.num_scheduled_tokens) == 256
    assert output.num_spec_tokens_to_schedule == 3


def test_scheduler_uses_static_k_when_no_requests_are_scheduled():
    scheduler = _make_scheduler_with_dynamic_sd(
        [(1, 16, 3), (64, 128, 2), (256, 4096, 0)],
        runtime_num_speculative_tokens=3,
    )
    output = scheduler.schedule()

    assert len(output.num_scheduled_tokens) == 0
    assert output.num_spec_tokens_to_schedule == 3

{
  "title": "Speculative runtime acceptance & rollback matrix",
  "owner": "Daniel Kim",
  "drive_area": "shared_drives",
  "path": "shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/speculative-runtime-acceptance-rollback-matrix.json",
  "doc_type": "doc",
  "created_at": "2026-02-14",
  "last_modified": "2026-03-10",
  "collaborators": [
    "Aisha Patel",
    "Lina Chen",
    "Marco Ruiz",
    "Eve Thompson"
  ],
  "team": "eng-serving-runtime",
  "status": "in_review",
  "tags": [
    "speculative-decoding",
    "kernels",
    "scheduler",
    "kv-cache",
    "rollout",
    "acceptance-metrics"
  ],
  "linked_artifacts": [
    "confluence:SERVE-SPEC-312",
    "jira:INF-7421",
    "github:redwood-inference/serving-runtime#1987",
    "doc:speculative-decode-integration-playbook.json"
  ],
  "summary": "Draft design and operational checklist for integrating speculative decoding into the runtime, including kernel selection heuristics, scheduler changes, KV cache behavior, acceptance criteria, rollback triggers, and the metrics to observably validate correctness and performance.",
  "background": "We want to deploy speculative decoding to reduce tail latency for large autoregressive requests while preserving cost constraints and model quality. Speculative decoding introduces multi-path execution, temporary duplication of work (speculative prefixes), and a dependency on fast kernel selection and cache coherence. This doc captures a pragmatic integration approach and an operational matrix for rollout and rollback.",
  "goals": "1) Reduce p95 token latency for long-context generator flows by >=20% on target workloads. 2) Maintain token cost delta <= +8% at steady state. 3) No detectable quality regression on critical eval sets (<=1% delta in quality score). 4) Provide clear rollback triggers and automated safeguards.",
  "non_goals": "1) Full redesign of kernel ABI. 2) Handling of all research variants of speculative algorithms (this is pragmatic production variant only).",
  "proposed_changes": "Introduce a speculative execution path in the request pipeline that can spawn a cheap fast-model speculative head alongside the main model; add a scheduler priority class for speculative work; extend KV cache semantics to support ephemeral speculative keys and a small pinned prefix cache for hot prompts; add kernel probing to select optimal attention/MatMul kernels for speculative fragments based on sequence length and quantization format.",
  "kernel_strategy": "Rule-based selection: 1) Probe at model load for supported kernels by sequence-length buckets (<=64, 65-512, >512) and quantization mode (fp16/int8/q4). 2) Maintain small per-model kernel preference table that maps (sequence_bucket, layer_type) -> kernel_id. 3) At runtime, for speculative fragments we prefer lowest-latency kernels with acceptable accuracy profiles; fallback to stable kernel for finalization. 4) Periodic background rebenchmarking during low load to refresh preferences.",
  "scheduler_changes": "1) Add 'speculative' priority queue that is preemptible and best-effort. 2) Speculative tasks get lower memory reservation; if main request completes earlier, speculative result is discarded. 3) Implement speculative concurrency limit per GPU (default 2 per-GPU) to bound resource amplification. 4) Batching: allow speculative fragments to join small fast batches (batch cap 8) while main model uses standard batching.",
  "kv_cache_design": "1) Two-tier KV cache per model: pinned-prefix cache (small, ~8MB per-shard) for common prompts and ephemeral speculative cache for in-flight speculative fragments. 2) Ephemeral cache entries have TTL tied to request lifetime and do not persist across requests. 3) Eviction: LRU for pinned-prefix; ephemeral entries are deallocated immediately after speculative path completes or is cancelled. 4) Consistency: when a speculative fragment produces KV state that is later used by main model, we support a fast copy path into persistent KV region only after verification step. 5) Metrics expose kv_pinned_hit_rate and kv_ephemeral_hit_rate.",
  "acceptance_criteria": "Functional: 1) Speculative path produces stable outputs that can be validated by merge logic in 99.9% of test requests in unit harness. 2) No memory leaks after 48h soak on canary hosts. Performance: 1) p95 token latency improves >=20% on synthetic long-tail workload with 90th percentile seq length >256. 2) End-to-end token cost increase <=8% compared to baseline. Quality: 1) Eval suite (regression-prompts-v2) shows <=1% drop in quality score. Observability: 1) All speculative metrics emitted (speculative_attempts, speculative_success_rate, speculative_waste_ratio, kv_pinned_hit_rate, kv_ephemeral_hit_rate). {
  "document": {
    "id": "dsid_b11cef8f59334594904e90f18be4739b",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/prompt-sets-and-benchmarks/top-hosted-models-benchmark-suite-v3.json",
    "title": "Top Hosted Models Benchmark Suite v3 (Prompt Sets + Workload Distributions)",
    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Top Hosted Models Benchmark Suite v3 (Prompt Sets + Workload Distributions)\",\n  \"space\": \"applied-ml-and-evals\",\n  \"author\": \"Claire Dubois\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-02-05\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-02-19\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Jonas Weber\",\n    \"Arjun Desai\",\n    \"Rina Kobayashi\",\n    \"Noah Patel\",\n    \"Allison Grant\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"benchmarks\",\n    \"evals\",\n    \"prompt-sets\",\n    \"hosted-models\",\n    \"fp8\",\n    \"int8\",\n    \"methodology\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"confluence://eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-benchmarking-methodology-top-hosted-models\",\n    \"confluence://architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/benchmarking-standards-fp8-int8\",\n    \"confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/fp8-int8-profile-policy-for-hosted-catalog\",\n    \"confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/fp8-int8-regression-triage-playbook\",\n    \"confluence://eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/fp8-int8-benchmark-dashboards\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"## 1. Purpose\\nThis document defines **Benchmark Suite v3** used for performance benchmarking and quality sanity checks across Redwood\\u2019s **top hosted models**. The suite is designed for:\\n\\n- **Kernel comparisons** (FP16/BF16 baseline vs FP8/INT8 variants) under realistic request shapes.\\n- **End-to-end serving benchmarks** (TTFT/TPOT/throughput) with representative prompt and generation-length distributions.\\n- **Quantization safety**: a lightweight quality sanity layer to catch obvious regressions (formatting, tool-call validity, long-context behavior).\\n\\nSuite v3 is explicitly aligned to production traffic patterns observed on the hosted API, while avoiding inclusion of customer-proprietary content.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 2. Scope and non-goals\\n### In scope\\n- Chat + instruction following\\n- RAG-like prompts (retrieval context included)\\n- Summarization + extraction\\n- Code generation + edit\\n- Structured output (JSON schemas)\\n- Tool-calling style prompts (function arguments)\\n- Short-form classification/labeling\\n- Long-context stress cases (prefill-heavy)\\n\\n### Not in scope (tracked separately)\\n- Multimodal inputs\\n- Fine-tuned customer prompts\\n- Domain-specific evals (legal/medical), unless requested by PM/CS for a specific launch\\n- Safety/policy compliance scoring (owned by Safety program; can be layered on top)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 3. Design principles\\n1) **Traffic representativeness**\\n- Suite composition (workload mix + prompt/generation lengths) approximates the hosted API\\u2019s request distribution for top models.\\n- We intentionally include a small number of \\u201ctail\\u201d cases (long context, structured output) because they materially impact p95 latency and kernel behavior.\\n\\n2) **Kernel sensitivity**\\n- Prompts are chosen to induce common shape regimes that matter for kernels:\\n  - Small/medium/large prefills\\n  - Decode lengths spanning short (32\\u2013128 tokens) to medium/long (512\\u20131024 tokens)\\n  - Attention patterns that stress KV-cache and memory bandwidth\\n\\n3) **Reproducibility**\\n- Deterministic prompt ordering, stable random seeds for sampling, and explicit versioning.\\n- Prompts are stored internally with immutable IDs; suite definitions reference IDs and weights.\\n\\n4) **No customer data**\\n- Prompts are synthetic or sourced from permissible open datasets and then rewritten/normalized.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 4. Suite composition (workloads)\\nSuite v3 is split into **six workload groups**. Each benchmark run uses the configured workload mix (Section 5) unless explicitly overridden.\\n\\n### 4.1 Chat (general assistant)\\n**Goal:** representative \\u201cdefault chat\\u201d traffic (balanced prefill/decode).\\n- Prompt style: user asks for explanation, brainstorming, or step-by-step guidance.\\n- Typical system prompt included (short, Redwood-default style).\\n- Output: natural language.\\n\\n### 4.2 RAG-style QA (context-in-prompt)\\n**Goal:** represent retrieval-augmented prompts where the prefill dominates.\\n- Prompt includes: instruction + question + 1\\u20134 context chunks (1\\u20133k tokens typical).\\n- Output: short answer + citations-like formatting (not strict).\\n\\n### 4.3 Summarization + extraction\\n**Goal:** common enterprise and product workloads; tests long prefill + medium decode.\\n- Inputs: meeting notes, policy snippets, support ticket-like text (synthetic).\\n- Outputs:\\n  - Summaries (bulleted)\\n  - Key points\\n  - Extraction (entities, action items)\\n\\n### 4.4 Code generation + edit\\n**Goal:** code models and code-heavy prompts stress different token distributions and may shift decode behavior.\\n- Prompts:\\n  - Generate a function from a spec\\n  - Refactor/edit an existing function (input includes code)\\n  - Fix a bug given failing test description\\n- Output: code blocks, sometimes multi-file pseudo-structure.\\n\\n### 4.5 Structured output (JSON)\\n**Goal:** enforce schema adherence; catches quantization-induced formatting drift.\\n- Prompts include a schema and strict instructions.\\n- Output must be valid JSON (no trailing commentary).\\n- Includes:\\n  - Simple schema (flat fields)\\n  - Nested schema (objects + arrays)\\n\\n### 4.6 Tool-calling (function arguments)\\n**Goal:** approximate tool-call patterns without relying on any single SDK; measures latency impact and validity of arguments.\\n- Prompts request selecting a tool and producing a JSON-like argument object.\\n- Validation checks:\\n  - Valid JSON\\n  - Required fields present\\n  - Basic type checks (string/number/bool/array)\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 5. Workload mix + distributions\\n### 5.1 High-level workload weights (default)\\nThe default suite mix is weighted to approximate hosted traffic for top models:\\n\\n- Chat (general): **35%**\\n- RAG-style QA: **20%**\\n- Summarization + extraction: **15%**\\n- Code generation/edit: **10%**\\n- Structured output (JSON): **10%**\\n- Tool-calling: **10%**\\n\\nRationale: Chat dominates absolute volume; RAG and summarization materially influence capacity planning due to heavier prefills; structured output/tool calling are smaller by volume but high-sensitivity for customer-visible correctness.\\n\\n### 5.2 Prompt length distribution (approximate)\\nPrompt lengths are measured as **model tokens after formatting** (system + user + any inserted context).\\n\\nDefault prompt-length buckets:\\n- **S (short): 64\\u2013256 tokens** \\u2192 25% of requests\\n- **M (medium): 256\\u20131,024 tokens** \\u2192 45% of requests\\n- **L (long): 1,024\\u20134,096 tokens** \\u2192 25% of requests\\n- **XL (very long): 4,096\\u201312,288 tokens** \\u2192 5% of requests\\n\\nNotes:\\n- XL is intentionally small but present to capture long-context TTFT behavior and KV-cache pressure.\\n- RAG workload draws more heavily from L/XL buckets; chat draws more heavily from S/M.\\n\\n### 5.3 Generation length distribution\\nGeneration lengths are capped and sampled per request. Default decode buckets:\\n- **32\\u2013128 tokens** \\u2192 40%\\n- **128\\u2013384 tokens** \\u2192 35%\\n- **384\\u2013768 tokens** \\u2192 20%\\n- **768\\u20131,024 tokens** \\u2192 5%\\n\\nRationale: Many hosted applications are short/medium responses; the long tail exists and matters for TPOT and sustained throughput.\\n\\n### 5.4 Prefill vs decode emphasis (why kernels care)\\nWe categorize suite cases by **prefill-heavy** vs **decode-heavy** shapes:\\n- Prefill-heavy (RAG, long summarization): drives TTFT and attention/matmul prefill kernels.\\n- Decode-heavy (short prompts, long generation): drives TPOT and decode attention kernels, KV-cache access, and launch overhead.\\n\\nIn Suite v3, approximately **55\\u201365% of total compute time** (not request count) is prefill, depending on model and batching configuration.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 6. Prompt sets (what\\u2019s inside)\\n### 6.1 Prompt library structure\\nSuite v3 references prompt IDs from the internal prompt library:\\n- Namespace: `aml_eval_prompts/hosted_suite/v3/`\\n- Each prompt has:\\n  - `prompt_id` (immutable)\\n  - `workload_group` (Section 4)\\n  - `length_bucket` target (S/M/L/XL)\\n  - `language` (mostly English; small multilingual slice)\\n  - `format_requirements` (none/json/tool)\\n  - `safety_notes` (if any)\\n\\n### 6.2 Multilingual slice\\nA small multilingual slice is included to reflect production usage without dominating the suite:\\n- **5%** of requests are non-English:\\n  - Spanish (2%)\\n  - French (1%)\\n  - German (1%)\\n  - Japanese (1%)\\n\\nThis slice is primarily in Chat + Summarization groups.\\n\\n### 6.3 Redaction and licensing\\n- No customer text.\\n- Sources are synthetic or derived from permissive corpora; rewritten where needed.\\n- Any prompt containing \\u201crealistic ticket/customer\\u201d patterns is fully synthetic.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 7. Structured-output and tool-calling variants\\n### 7.1 Structured JSON tasks\\nTwo levels are used:\\n\\n**JSON-Simple** (approx. half of structured-output cases)\\n- 6\\u201310 fields\\n- Mostly strings + integers\\n- Example use cases: extraction, metadata normalization\\n\\n**JSON-Nested** (approx. half)\\n- Arrays of objects, nested structures\\n- Example use cases: itinerary planning, task breakdowns, RAG citation objects\\n\\nValidation rules:\\n- Must parse as JSON\\n- Must contain required keys\\n- No extra keys when `additionalProperties=false` (where defined)\\n\\n### 7.2 Tool-calling tasks\\nTool calls are represented as \\u201cproduce the arguments for tool X\\u201d prompts, where tool X is described in the prompt.\\n\\nTool set (representative):\\n- `search_documents(query, top_k, filters)`\\n- `create_ticket(title, description, severity, tags)`\\n- `schedule_meeting(attendees, start_time, duration_minutes, agenda)`\\n\\nValidation rules:\\n- Valid JSON\\n- Required fields present\\n- Simple type checks\\n\\nWhy this is included in perf benchmarking:\\n- Tool calling is sensitive to **formatting and small-token probabilities** (quantization can cause increased invalid JSON rates).\\n- These cases are often latency-sensitive in production because they block downstream actions.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 8. How the suite is used in benchmarking\\n### 8.1 Benchmark modes\\nSuite v3 supports two primary modes:\\n\\n1) **E2E Serving Mode (recommended for sprint decisions)**\\n- Runs through the serving stack with realistic scheduler behavior.\\n- Captures TTFT, TPOT, tokens/sec, queueing, and error rates.\\n\\n2) **Microbench Assist Mode (kernel shape coverage)**\\n- Uses extracted shapes from Suite v3 tokenization to drive targeted matmul/attention microbenches.\\n- Used to explain wins/regressions seen in E2E.\\n\\n### 8.2 Standard run parameters (defaults)\\nUnless a methodology page overrides, use:\\n- Temperature: 0.0 for structured output/tool calling; 0.2 for chat-style tasks\\n- Top_p: 1.0\\n- Frequency/presence penalty: 0\\n- Stop sequences: workload-specific (JSON/tool modes enforce strict stops)\\n- Streaming: enabled for E2E mode where applicable (TTFT is primary metric)\\n\\n### 8.3 Concurrency and batching\\nThe suite is designed to be executed under multiple load points (owned by runtime benchmarking methodology). Suite v3 itself provides the **request shape distribution**; scheduling tests should vary:\\n- concurrency (e.g., 1, 8, 32)\\n- batching windows\\n- prefill/decode mixing policy\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 9. Quality sanity checks (minimum required)\\nSuite v3 includes lightweight checks to detect obvious regressions when enabling FP8/INT8.\\n\\nRequired checks by workload:\\n- Chat/RAG/Summarization/Code: heuristic checks (non-empty, no repeated garbage, length sanity) + spot-check sampling\\n- Structured JSON: strict JSON parse + schema validation\\n- Tool-calling: strict JSON parse + required fields/type checks\\n\\nMinimum acceptance guidelines (for default enablement proposals):\\n- JSON validity rate: **>= 99.5%** on JSON tasks\\n- Tool-arg validity rate: **>= 99.0%** on tool tasks\\n- No new systematic failure mode (e.g., truncation, invalid unicode, persistent repetition) in spot-check sample\\n\\nAny proposed default change (FP8/INT8) must also comply with the quantization policy sign-off criteria.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 10. Versioning, change control, and auditability\\n### 10.1 Versioning rules\\n- Suite version is `vMAJOR.MINOR` (this doc is v3; minor bumps allowed for prompt additions/removals without rebalancing weights).\\n- Any change that affects distributions (weights, length buckets, multilingual %) requires a **MINOR bump** and explicit rationale.\\n- Any substantial redesign requires a **MAJOR bump**.\\n\\n### 10.2 Change approval\\nApprovers:\\n- Applied ML/Evals: **Jonas Weber** (decision owner)\\n- Serving Runtime Harness: **Rina Kobayashi** (integration owner)\\n- Perf Standards: **Noah Patel** (for any external-claim implications)\\n\\n### 10.3 Reproducibility metadata\\nEvery run that claims Suite v3 compliance must record:\\n- suite version (e.g., `hosted_suite_v3.0`)\\n- prompt library revision hash\\n- sampling seed\\n- tokenizer/model revision hash\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 11. Rationale: why this matches production traffic\\nSuite v3 matches production behavior because:\\n- It reproduces the dominant workload classes (chat + RAG + summarization) and includes smaller but high-impact classes (structured output/tool calling).\\n- The prompt-length and generation-length distributions approximate observed hosted traffic shape regimes, including long-context tail cases that influence p95 and kernel selection.\\n- It covers both prefill-heavy and decode-heavy regimes, which is necessary to make correct decisions about kernel auto-selection and scheduler tuning.\\n- It includes strict formatting tasks to catch the failure modes most likely to become customer-visible during quantized rollouts.\\n\\nKnown limitations:\\n- True customer prompt diversity is broader than any fixed suite; this is a representative benchmark, not a guarantee.\\n- Some domains (highly technical, regulated) are underrepresented; request an add-on suite if needed for a specific customer/launch.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 12. Quick reference: Suite v3 defaults\\n- Workload mix: 35% chat / 20% RAG / 15% summarize+extract / 10% code / 10% JSON / 10% tool\\n- Prompt length buckets: 25% S / 45% M / 25% L / 5% XL\\n- Generation buckets: 40% (32\\u2013128) / 35% (128\\u2013384) / 20% (384\\u2013768) / 5% (768\\u20131024)\\n- Multilingual: 5% total (ES/FR/DE/JA)\\n- Required quality sanity: JSON >= 99.5%, tool args >= 99.0%\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 13. Contact / ownership\\n- Primary owner: **Applied ML & Evals** (Jonas Weber)\\n- Prompt set curator: **Claire Dubois**\\n- Harness integration: **Rina Kobayashi**\\n\\nFor issues (prompt bugs, distribution mismatches, validity regressions), file an issue under the FP8/INT8 sprint epic and tag `#eng-ml` + `#eng-runtime`.\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_b11cef8f59334594904e90f18be4739b\"\n}",

{
  "title": "Top Hosted Models Benchmark Suite v3 (Prompt Sets + Workload Distributions)",
  "space": "applied-ml-and-evals",
  "author": "Claire Dubois",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-02-05",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-19",
  "reviewers": [
    "Jonas Weber",
    "Arjun Desai",
    "Rina Kobayashi",
    "Noah Patel",
    "Allison Grant"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "benchmarks",
    "evals",
    "prompt-sets",
    "hosted-models",
    "fp8",
    "int8",
    "methodology"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "related_pages": [
    "confluence://eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/kernel-benchmarking-methodology-top-hosted-models",
    "confluence://architecture-and-standards/performance-standards/benchmarking-standards-fp8-int8",
    "confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/quantization-profiles/fp8-int8-profile-policy-for-hosted-catalog",
    "confluence://applied-ml-and-evals/regression-triage/fp8-int8-regression-triage-playbook",
    "confluence://eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/fp8-int8-benchmark-dashboards"
  ],
  "content": "## 1. Purpose
This document defines **Benchmark Suite v3** used for performance benchmarking and quality sanity checks across Redwood’s **top hosted models**. The suite is designed for:

- **Kernel comparisons** (FP16/BF16 baseline vs FP8/INT8 variants) under realistic request shapes.
- **End-to-end serving benchmarks** (TTFT/TPOT/throughput) with representative prompt and generation-length distributions.
- **Quantization safety**: a lightweight quality sanity layer to catch obvious regressions (formatting, tool-call validity, long-context behavior).

Suite v3 is explicitly aligned to production traffic patterns observed on the hosted API, while avoiding inclusion of customer-proprietary content.

---

## 2. Scope and non-goals
### In scope
- Chat + instruction following
- RAG-like prompts (retrieval context included)
- Summarization + extraction
- Code generation + edit
- Structured output (JSON schemas)
- Tool-calling style prompts (function arguments)
- Short-form classification/labeling
- Long-context stress cases (prefill-heavy)

### Not in scope (tracked separately)
- Multimodal inputs
- Fine-tuned customer prompts
- Domain-specific evals (legal/medical), unless requested by PM/CS for a specific launch
- Safety/policy compliance scoring (owned by Safety program; can be layered on top)

---

## 3. Design principles
1) **Traffic representativeness**
- Suite composition (workload mix + prompt/generation lengths) approximates the hosted API’s request distribution for top models.
- We intentionally include a small number of “tail” cases (long context, structured output) because they materially impact p95 latency and kernel behavior.

2) **Kernel sensitivity**
- Prompts are chosen to induce common shape regimes that matter for kernels:
  - Small/medium/large prefills
  - Decode lengths spanning short (32–128 tokens) to medium/long (512–1024 tokens)
  - Attention patterns that stress KV-cache and memory bandwidth

3) **Reproducibility**
- Deterministic prompt ordering, stable random seeds for sampling, and explicit versioning.
- Prompts are stored internally with immutable IDs; suite definitions reference IDs and weights.

4) **No customer data**
- Prompts are synthetic or sourced from permissible open datasets and then rewritten/normalized.

---

## 4. Suite composition (workloads)
Suite v3 is split into **six workload groups**. Each benchmark run uses the configured workload mix (Section 5) unless explicitly overridden.

### 4.1 Chat (general assistant)
**Goal:** representative “default chat” traffic (balanced prefill/decode).
- Prompt style: user asks for explanation, brainstorming, or step-by-step guidance.
- Typical system prompt included (short, Redwood-default style).
- Output: natural language.

### 4.2 RAG-style QA (context-in-prompt)
**Goal:** represent retrieval-augmented prompts where the prefill dominates.
- Prompt includes: instruction + question + 1–4 context chunks (1–3k tokens typical).
- Output: short answer + citations-like formatting (not strict).

### 4.3 Summarization + extraction
**Goal:** common enterprise and product workloads; tests long prefill + medium decode.
- Inputs: meeting notes, policy snippets, support ticket-like text (synthetic).
- Outputs:
  - Summaries (bulleted)
  - Key points
  - Extraction (entities, action items)

### 4.4 Code generation + edit
**Goal:** code models and code-heavy prompts stress different token distributions and may shift decode behavior.
- Prompts:
  - Generate a function from a spec
  - Refactor/edit an existing function (input includes code)
  - Fix a bug given failing test description
- Output: code blocks, sometimes multi-file pseudo-structure.

### 4.5 Structured output (JSON)
**Goal:** enforce schema adherence; catches quantization-induced formatting drift.
- Prompts include a schema and strict instructions.
- Output must be valid JSON (no trailing commentary).
- Includes:
  - Simple schema (flat fields)
  - Nested schema (objects + arrays)

### 4.6 Tool-calling (function arguments)
**Goal:** approximate tool-call patterns without relying on any single SDK; measures latency impact and validity of arguments.
- Prompts request selecting a tool and producing a JSON-like argument object.
- Validation checks:
  - Valid JSON
  - Required fields present
  - Basic type checks (string/number/bool/array)

---

## 5. Workload mix + distributions
### 5.1 High-level workload weights (default)
The default suite mix is weighted to approximate hosted traffic for top models:

- Chat (general): **35%**
- RAG-style QA: **20%**
- Summarization + extraction: **15%**
- Code generation/edit: **10%**
- Structured output (JSON): **10%**
- Tool-calling: **10%**

Rationale: Chat dominates absolute volume; RAG and summarization materially influence capacity planning due to heavier prefills; structured output/tool calling are smaller by volume but high-sensitivity for customer-visible correctness.

### 5.2 Prompt length distribution (approximate)
Prompt lengths are measured as **model tokens after formatting** (system + user + any inserted context).

Default prompt-length buckets:
- **S (short): 64–256 tokens** → 25% of requests
- **M (medium): 256–1,024 tokens** → 45% of requests
- **L (long): 1,024–4,096 tokens** → 25% of requests
- **XL (very long): 4,096–12,288 tokens** → 5% of requests

Notes:
- XL is intentionally small but present to capture long-context TTFT behavior and KV-cache pressure.
- RAG workload draws more heavily from L/XL buckets; chat draws more heavily from S/M.

### 5.3 Generation length distribution
Generation lengths are capped and sampled per request. Default decode buckets:
- **32–128 tokens** → 40%
- **128–384 tokens** → 35%
- **384–768 tokens** → 20%
- **768–1,024 tokens** → 5%

Rationale: Many hosted applications are short/medium responses; the long tail exists and matters for TPOT and sustained throughput.

### 5.4 Prefill vs decode emphasis (why kernels care)
We categorize suite cases by **prefill-heavy** vs **decode-heavy** shapes:
- Prefill-heavy (RAG, long summarization): drives TTFT and attention/matmul prefill kernels.
- Decode-heavy (short prompts, long generation): drives TPOT and decode attention kernels, KV-cache access, and launch overhead.

In Suite v3, approximately **55–65% of total compute time** (not request count) is prefill, depending on model and batching configuration.

---

## 6. Prompt sets (what’s inside)
### 6.1 Prompt library structure
Suite v3 references prompt IDs from the internal prompt library:
- Namespace: `aml_eval_prompts/hosted_suite/v3/`
- Each prompt has:
  - `prompt_id` (immutable)
  - `workload_group` (Section 4)
  - `length_bucket` target (S/M/L/XL)
  - `language` (mostly English; small multilingual slice)
  - `format_requirements` (none/json/tool)
  - `safety_notes` (if any)

### 6.2 Multilingual slice
A small multilingual slice is included to reflect production usage without dominating the suite:
- **5%** of requests are non-English:
  - Spanish (2%)
  - French (1%)
  - German (1%)
  - Japanese (1%)

This slice is primarily in Chat + Summarization groups.

### 6.3 Redaction and licensing
- No customer text.
- Sources are synthetic or derived from permissive corpora; rewritten where needed.
- Any prompt containing “realistic ticket/customer” patterns is fully synthetic.

---

## 7. Structured-output and tool-calling variants
### 7.1 Structured JSON tasks
Two levels are used:

**JSON-Simple** (approx. half of structured-output cases)
- 6–10 fields
- Mostly strings + integers
- Example use cases: extraction, metadata normalization

**JSON-Nested** (approx. half)
- Arrays of objects, nested structures
- Example use cases: itinerary planning, task breakdowns, RAG citation objects

Validation rules:
- Must parse as JSON
- Must contain required keys
- No extra keys when `additionalProperties=false` (where defined)

### 7.2 Tool-calling tasks
Tool calls are represented as “produce the arguments for tool X” prompts, where tool X is described in the prompt.

Tool set (representative):
- `search_documents(query, top_k, filters)`
- `create_ticket(title, description, severity, tags)`
- `schedule_meeting(attendees, start_time, duration_minutes, agenda)`

Validation rules:
- Valid JSON
- Required fields present
- Simple type checks

Why this is included in perf benchmarking:
- Tool calling is sensitive to **formatting and small-token probabilities** (quantization can cause increased invalid JSON rates).
- These cases are often latency-sensitive in production because they block downstream actions.

---

## 8. How the suite is used in benchmarking
### 8.1 Benchmark modes
Suite v3 supports two primary modes:

1) **E2E Serving Mode (recommended for sprint decisions)**
- Runs through the serving stack with realistic scheduler behavior.
- Captures TTFT, TPOT, tokens/sec, queueing, and error rates.

2) **Microbench Assist Mode (kernel shape coverage)**
- Uses extracted shapes from Suite v3 tokenization to drive targeted matmul/attention microbenches.
- Used to explain wins/regressions seen in E2E.

### 8.2 Standard run parameters (defaults)
Unless a methodology page overrides, use:
- Temperature: 0.0 for structured output/tool calling; 0.2 for chat-style tasks
- Top_p: 1.0
- Frequency/presence penalty: 0
- Stop sequences: workload-specific (JSON/tool modes enforce strict stops)
- Streaming: enabled for E2E mode where applicable (TTFT is primary metric)

### 8.3 Concurrency and batching
The suite is designed to be executed under multiple load points (owned by runtime benchmarking methodology). Suite v3 itself provides the **request shape distribution**; scheduling tests should vary:
- concurrency (e.g., 1, 8, 32)
- batching windows
- prefill/decode mixing policy

---

## 9. Quality sanity checks (minimum required)
Suite v3 includes lightweight checks to detect obvious regressions when enabling FP8/INT8.

Required checks by workload:
- Chat/RAG/Summarization/Code: heuristic checks (non-empty, no repeated garbage, length sanity) + spot-check sampling
- Structured JSON: strict JSON parse + schema validation
- Tool-calling: strict JSON parse + required fields/type checks

Minimum acceptance guidelines (for default enablement proposals):
- JSON validity rate: **>= 99.5%** on JSON tasks
- Tool-arg validity rate: **>= 99.0%** on tool tasks
- No new systematic failure mode (e.g., truncation, invalid unicode, persistent repetition) in spot-check sample

Any proposed default change (FP8/INT8) must also comply with the quantization policy sign-off criteria.

---

## 10. Versioning, change control, and auditability
### 10.1 Versioning rules
- Suite version is `vMAJOR.MINOR` (this doc is v3; minor bumps allowed for prompt additions/removals without rebalancing weights).
- Any change that affects distributions (weights, length buckets, multilingual %) requires a **MINOR bump** and explicit rationale.
- Any substantial redesign requires a **MAJOR bump**.

### 10.2 Change approval
Approvers:
- Applied ML/Evals: **Jonas Weber** (decision owner)
- Serving Runtime Harness: **Rina Kobayashi** (integration owner)
- Perf Standards: **Noah Patel** (for any external-claim implications)

### 10.3 Reproducibility metadata
Every run that claims Suite v3 compliance must record:
- suite version (e.g., `hosted_suite_v3.0`)
- prompt library revision hash
- sampling seed
- tokenizer/model revision hash

---

## 11. Rationale: why this matches production traffic
Suite v3 matches production behavior because:
- It reproduces the dominant workload classes (chat + RAG + summarization) and includes smaller but high-impact classes (structured output/tool calling).
- The prompt-length and generation-length distributions approximate observed hosted traffic shape regimes, including long-context tail cases that influence p95 and kernel selection.
- It covers both prefill-heavy and decode-heavy regimes, which is necessary to make correct decisions about kernel auto-selection and scheduler tuning.
- It includes strict formatting tasks to catch the failure modes most likely to become customer-visible during quantized rollouts.

Known limitations:
- True customer prompt diversity is broader than any fixed suite; this is a representative benchmark, not a guarantee.
- Some domains (highly technical, regulated) are underrepresented; request an add-on suite if needed for a specific customer/launch.

---

## 12. Quick reference: Suite v3 defaults
- Workload mix: 35% chat / 20% RAG / 15% summarize+extract / 10% code / 10% JSON / 10% tool
- Prompt length buckets: 25% S / 45% M / 25% L / 5% XL
- Generation buckets: 40% (32–128) / 35% (128–384) / 20% (384–768) / 5% (768–1024)
- Multilingual: 5% total (ES/FR/DE/JA)
- Required quality sanity: JSON >= 99.5%, tool args >= 99.0%

---

## 13. Contact / ownership
- Primary owner: **Applied ML & Evals** (Jonas Weber)
- Prompt set curator: **Claire Dubois**
- Harness integration: **Rina Kobayashi**

For issues (prompt bugs, distribution mismatches, validity regressions), file an issue under the FP8/INT8 sprint epic and tag `#eng-ml` + `#eng-runtime`.",

    "id": "dsid_cf59c9d7c95d4cd184713088627f2e37",

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/google_drive",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Speculative Decoding + Model Onboarding: runtime draft and rollback plan\",\n  \"owner\": \"Aisha Patel\",\n  \"drive_area\": \"shared_drives\",\n  \"path\": \"shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/speculative-decoding-model-onboarding-draft.json\",\n  \"doc_type\": \"doc\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2024-11-07\",\n  \"last_modified\": \"2024-11-20\",\n  \"collaborators\": [\n    \"Daniel Cho\",\n    \"Mariana Ruiz\",\n    \"Evan Green\"\n  ],\n  \"team\": \"eng-serving-runtime\",\n  \"status\": \"draft\",\n  \"tags\": [\n    \"speculative-decoding\",\n    \"kv-cache\",\n    \"scheduling\",\n    \"model-onboarding\",\n    \"rollback\",\n    \"metrics\"\n  ],\n  \"linked_artifacts\": [\n    \"https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INFR/Speculative+Decoding+Notes\",\n    \"JIRA-2034\",\n    \"github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1123\"\n  ],\n  \"content\": \"Purpose and scope:\\\\nThis document captures a working design for integrating speculative decoding into the serving runtime and the associated acceptance/rollback and metrics plan for onboarding model variants. It focuses on interactions between kernel execution, the KV cache, the scheduler, and model integration lifecycle (canary -> rollout -> rollback).\\\\n\\\\nGoals:\\\\n- Specify concrete semantics for speculative decoding in multi-kernel environments.\\\\n- Describe scheduling invariants so speculative batches don't violate latency SLOs for non-speculative traffic.\\\\n- Define KV cache coherence and eviction rules under speculative execution.\\\\n- Provide model acceptance criteria, telemetry, and automated rollback triggers specific to speculative changes.\\\\n\\\\nHigh-level idea:\\\\nSpeculative decoding issues a small number of ahead-of-time token continuations using a cheaper/softer model or optimized kernel path to reduce perceived latency for single-turn and streaming workloads. If the low-cost speculation matches the final generation, we serve the content immediately; otherwise we splice or replace tokens when the authoritative path completes.\\\\n\\\\nKey constraints to keep in mind:\\\\n- Never expose tokens that the customer did not authorize per route-level config; speculation must be opt-in per model/route.\\\\n- Speculation must not increase P99 tail for high-priority routes above configured SLO delta.\\\\n- Cache correctness: speculative and authoritative KV cache entries must be properly versioned to avoid stale KV re-use across divergent paths.\\\\n\\\\nSpeculative execution modes (planned):\\\\n1) Soft-speculate (same model, cheaper kernel): run inexpensive quantized kernel to produce the next N tokens while the full-precision kernel is spinning up CPU/GPU.\\\\n2) Model-speculate (smaller model): run a distilled/smaller model to predict next tokens; later confirm with primary model.\\\\n3) Hybrid (cached prefix + soft-speculate): for requests matching cached prefixes, use KV cache + cheap kernel to extend tokens.\\\\n\\\\nRuntime components touched:\\\\n- Scheduler: responsible for deciding whether to allocate a speculative task slot.\\\\n- Kernel selector: must support marking runs as speculative and exposing confidence metrics (logits gap / max-softmax / entropy).\\\\n- KV cache: must store speculative entries separately and support commit/merge/abort semantics.\\\\n- Streamer and client protocol: must support speculative token markers so downstream clients can display tentative tokens if configured.\\\\n\\\\nScheduler changes and invariants:\\\\n- Speculative work is explicitly lower priority and preemptible. Scheduler must enforce:\\\\n  - Soft cap: speculative GPU utilization <= 15% per serving-instance by default.\\\\n  - Preemption policy: if speculative work threatens SLOs for non-speculative traffic, in-progress speculative tasks should be cancelled at token-boundary (cooperative cancellation).\\\\n  - Admission control: only allow speculative runs when headroom (latency SLA margin) exists for the current traffic mix. Headroom computed from moving-window latency percentiles and configured safety margin.\\\\n- Fairness: do not allow speculative runs for premium routes unless route config enables it.\\\\n\\\\nKernel and execution semantics:\\\\n- Kernels must annotate speculative outputs with a speculation_id and a confidence vector summary (top-3 token probs, entropy).\\\\n- No in-place mutations of KV cache by speculative kernels. Speculative kernels write to a speculative-layer in-memory store keyed by (request_id, speculation_id, kv_key).\\\\n- When full model run completes, runtime compares speculative-layer entries and authoritative outputs; on match (token-level equality for the speculative window) speculative entries are committed to canonical KV cache; on mismatch the speculative-layer is discarded and authoritative entries take effect.\\\\n- To avoid double-counting usage, speculative tokens are accounted separately and can be optionally billable at a discounted speculative rate.\\\\n\\\\nKV cache design for speculative flows:\\\\n- Two-layer model: committed layer (canonical) + speculative overlay(s). Overlays are ordered by speculation start time.\\\\n- Read semantics: read prefers the topmost overlay for keys that match request_id scope when reading during an in-flight speculative-confirmation round. After commit/abort, overlay entries are merged or dropped.\\\\n- Eviction: overlays have their own TTL and size cap (we cap overlay size per-request to limit memory pressure). If eviction happens before commit, speculation is treated as aborted.\\\\n- Versioning: each KV key gets a monotonic sequence id per-request; overlays include sequence ranges so merges are efficient (append-only semantics where possible).\\\\n\\\\nModel onboarding, acceptance criteria, and rollout plan (speculation-aware):\\\\n- Canary policy: when onboarding a new model variant that will participate in speculation (e.g., a distilled spec model or new kernel variant), start with a 0.5% canary of traffic with speculation enabled. Two parallel flows: spec-enabled and spec-disabled to measure delta.\\\\n- Acceptance metrics (must be monitored and satisfy guardrails over 24h window unless otherwise specified):\\\\n  - Token-level divergence: fraction of speculative-token windows where authoritative tokens differ from speculative tokens (target: <= 6% for model-speculate; <= 1% for soft-speculate).\\\\n  - Commit rate: percentage of speculative windows that are committed vs aborted (target: >= 90% for soft-speculate; >= 70% for model-speculate).\\\\n  - Quality delta: A/B evals on downstream quality signals (e.g., Rouge/BLEU/LLM-specific evals on prompt sets). No statistically significant drop vs baseline (alpha=0.01).\\\\n  - Latency improvements: median client-perceived time-to-first-meaningful-token (TTFMT) should improve by >= 8% for spec-enabled traffic.\\\\n  - Resource overhead: additional GPU/VRAM utilization attributable to speculation <= 10% of baseline capacity at canary scale.\\\\n  - Error surface: speculative-specific errors (overlay evictions, preempted specs) must be < 0.1% of requests.\\\\n- Safety gates (automatic):\\\\n  - If token-level divergence > 10% over 1h, immediate rollback of speculation path for that model.\\\\n  - If commit rate < configured minimum for 30m (rolling), disable speculation for the model variant.\\\\n  - If P99 latency for non-spec traffic increases by > 5% absolute, preempt all speculation in impacted region/instance.\\\\n\\\\nRollback and canary isolation details:\\\\n- Rollback granularity: model_variant, region, pool, route. Can roll back speculation codepath for a model without removing the model entirely (configurable).\\\\n- Automated rollback flow:\\\\n  1) Detection triggers via metrics alerting rules.\\\\n  2) Orchestration layer marks the model variant/speculation flag as disabled and pushes policy to router/scheduler.\\\\n  3) Instances gracefully cancel speculative in-flight tasks (finish current token then abort speculative continuation) and invalidate overlays.\\\\n  4) Telemetry events emitted: speculation.rollback.triggered, speculation.rollback.completed, speculation.rollback.reason.\\\\n- Human-in-the-loop: we add a manual-confirm rollback for anything that affects >5% of traffic; automatic rollback for small canaries is allowed.\\\\n\\\\nObservability and telemetry (instrumentation plan):\\\\n- Core events (per-request dimensioned):\\\\n  - speculation.request.start {speculation_id, model_variant, mode, route, route_tier}\\\\n  - speculation.run.complete {speculation_id, outcome: committed|aborted|preempted|evicted, commit_latency_ms}\\\\n  - speculation.confidence.summary {entropy, max_logit_margin}\\\\n  - kv.overlay.merge {speculation_id, keys_merged}\\\\n  - speculation.rollback.{triggered|completed}\\\\n- Metrics to be derived:\\\\n  - speculation.commit_rate (per-model, per-route)\\\\n  - speculation.divergence_rate (per-model)\\\\n  - speculation.latency_benefit.p50/p95/p99 (client perceived)\\\\n  - speculation.cpu_gpu_overhead_pct (per-node)\\\\n- Dashboards and alerts:\\\\n  - Canary dashboard showing divergence vs quality evals, commit rate, and resource overhead.\\\\n  - SLO alerts: speculative_preemption_rate > threshold, divergence spikes, commit_rate drop.\\\\n\\\\nExample request flow (simplified):\\\\n1) Request arrives, route config indicates speculation allowed and selects mode=soft-speculate.\\\\n2) Scheduler checks headroom, admits speculative job into low-prio queue and allocates a quantized kernel slot.\\\\n3) Spec kernel runs and writes overlay entries for KV keys and emits speculation.request.start. Client receives tentative tokens with speculation markers.\\\\n4) Primary model kernel begins; reads committed cache + overlays. It produces authoritative tokens.\\\\n5) Primary kernel compares the token window with speculative output; if identical: overlay is committed; telemetry emits speculation.run.complete outcome=committed and overlay merge. If not identical: outcome=aborted and speculative tokens are replaced client-side where protocol allows, or authoritative tokens are appended with correction metadata.\\\\n\\\\nTesting and validation plan:\\\\n- Unit tests for overlay merge/abort semantics and eviction behavior.\\\\n- Integration tests simulating concurrent spec and authoritative runs with simulated preemption and cache eviction.\\\\n- Load tests at 0.5%, 5%, and 20% speculation intensity measuring latency tail and memory pressure.\\\\n- Golden prompt set: curated set of production prompts for automated divergence and quality checks.\\\\n\\\\nOpen questions / decisions needed:\\\\n- UI behavior: what is the default client experience when speculative tokens are later aborted? (options: visual rollback, replace text, show correction markers).\\\\n- Billing model: do we bill speculative tokens? If yes, at what discount? Need product/finance input.\\\\n- How to define per-route headroom safely for mixed-traffic environments? Propose starting conservative and exposing a route knob to opt into higher speculation caps.\\\\n- Kernel contract: how detailed should the confidence summary be for effective commit heuristics? (more telemetry increases overhead).\\\\n\\\\nAppendix: proposed rollout timeline (high level)\\\\n- Week 0-2: implement kernel and KV overlay primitives + unit tests.\\\\n- Week 3-4: local integration, overlay merging, and synthetic load tests.\\\\n- Week 5: internal dogfood on dev cluster with opt-in routes.\\\\n- Week 6-8: 0.5% canary for model variants + dashboards and alerts.\\\\n- Week 9-12: expand canary to 5% and run extended quality evals; iterate on acceptance thresholds.\\\\n\\\\nAction items:\\\\n- Product: confirm billing stance for speculative tokens (assigned: Mariana).\\\\n- Platform/SRE: define safe default headroom calculation and add scheduler admission control hooks (assigned: Evan).\\\\n- Serving runtime: prototype overlay KV API and speculative annotations in kernel interface (assigned: Daniel).\\\\n\\\\nIf we want, I can break this into a narrower PRD focusing only on KV overlay APIs or only on the scheduler admission control. For now this is intended as a cross-team working draft to iterate against concrete impl PRs.\\\\n\\\\nEnd of document.\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_cf59c9d7c95d4cd184713088627f2e37\"\n}",

document.content:
{
  "title": "Speculative Decoding + Model Onboarding: runtime draft and rollback plan",
  "owner": "Aisha Patel",
  "drive_area": "shared_drives",
  "path": "shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime/speculative-decoding-model-onboarding-draft.json",
  "doc_type": "doc",
  "created_at": "2024-11-07",
  "last_modified": "2024-11-20",
  "collaborators": [
    "Daniel Cho",
    "Mariana Ruiz",
    "Evan Green"
  ],
  "team": "eng-serving-runtime",
  "status": "draft",
  "tags": [
    "speculative-decoding",
    "kv-cache",
    "scheduling",
    "model-onboarding",
    "rollback",
    "metrics"
  ],
  "linked_artifacts": [
    "https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INFR/Speculative+Decoding+Notes",
    "JIRA-2034",
    "github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1123"
  ],
  "content": "Purpose and scope:\\nThis document captures a working design for integrating speculative decoding into the serving runtime and the associated acceptance/rollback and metrics plan for onboarding model variants. It focuses on interactions between kernel execution, the KV cache, the scheduler, and model integration lifecycle (canary -> rollout -> rollback).\\n\\nGoals:\\n- Specify concrete semantics for speculative decoding in multi-kernel environments.\\n- Describe scheduling invariants so speculative batches don't violate latency SLOs for non-speculative traffic.\\n- Define KV cache coherence and eviction rules under speculative execution.\\n- Provide model acceptance criteria, telemetry, and automated rollback triggers specific to speculative changes.\\n\\nHigh-level idea:\\nSpeculative decoding issues a small number of ahead-of-time token continuations using a cheaper/softer model or optimized kernel path to reduce perceived latency for single-turn and streaming workloads. If the low-cost speculation matches the final generation, we serve the content immediately; otherwise we splice or replace tokens when the authoritative path completes.\\n\\nKey constraints to keep in mind:\\n- Never expose tokens that the customer did not authorize per route-level config; speculation must be opt-in per model/route.\\n- Speculation must not increase P99 tail for high-priority routes above configured SLO delta.\\n- Cache correctness: speculative and authoritative KV cache entries must be properly versioned to avoid stale KV re-use across divergent paths.\\n\\nSpeculative execution modes (planned):\\n1) Soft-speculate (same model, cheaper kernel): run inexpensive quantized kernel to produce the next N tokens while the full-precision kernel is spinning up CPU/GPU.\\n2) Model-speculate (smaller model): run a distilled/smaller model to predict next tokens; later confirm with primary model.\\n3) Hybrid (cached prefix + soft-speculate): for requests matching cached prefixes, use KV cache + cheap kernel to extend tokens.\\n\\nRuntime components touched:\\n- Scheduler: responsible for deciding whether to allocate a speculative task slot.\\n- Kernel selector: must support marking runs as speculative and exposing confidence metrics (logits gap / max-softmax / entropy).\\n- KV cache: must store speculative entries separately and support commit/merge/abort semantics.\\n- Streamer and client protocol: must support speculative token markers so downstream clients can display tentative tokens if configured.\\n\\nScheduler changes and invariants:\\n- Speculative work is explicitly lower priority and preemptible. Scheduler must enforce:\\n  - Soft cap: speculative GPU utilization <= 15% per serving-instance by default.\\n  - Preemption policy: if speculative work threatens SLOs for non-speculative traffic, in-progress speculative tasks should be cancelled at token-boundary (cooperative cancellation).\\n  - Admission control: only allow speculative runs when headroom (latency SLA margin) exists for the current traffic mix. Headroom computed from moving-window latency percentiles and configured safety margin.\\n- Fairness: do not allow speculative runs for premium routes unless route config enables it.\\n\\nKernel and execution semantics:\\n- Kernels must annotate speculative outputs with a speculation_id and a confidence vector summary (top-3 token probs, entropy).\\n- No in-place mutations of KV cache by speculative kernels. Speculative kernels write to a speculative-layer in-memory store keyed by (request_id, speculation_id, kv_key).\\n- When full model run completes, runtime compares speculative-layer entries and authoritative outputs; on match (token-level equality for the speculative window) speculative entries are committed to canonical KV cache; on mismatch the speculative-layer is discarded and authoritative entries take effect.\\n- To avoid double-counting usage, speculative tokens are accounted separately and can be optionally billable at a discounted speculative rate.\\n\\nKV cache design for speculative flows:\\n- Two-layer model: committed layer (canonical) + speculative overlay(s). Overlays are ordered by speculation start time.\\n- Read semantics: read prefers the topmost overlay for keys that match request_id scope when reading during an in-flight speculative-confirmation round. After commit/abort, overlay entries are merged or dropped.\\n- Eviction: overlays have their own TTL and size cap (we cap overlay size per-request to limit memory pressure). If eviction happens before commit, speculation is treated as aborted.\\n- Versioning: each KV key gets a monotonic sequence id per-request; overlays include sequence ranges so merges are efficient (append-only semantics where possible).\\n\\nModel onboarding, acceptance criteria, and rollout plan (speculation-aware):\\n- Canary policy: when onboarding a new model variant that will participate in speculation (e.g., a distilled spec model or new kernel variant), start with a 0.5% canary of traffic with speculation enabled. Two parallel flows: spec-enabled and spec-disabled to measure delta.\\n- Acceptance metrics (must be monitored and satisfy guardrails over 24h window unless otherwise specified):\\n  - Token-level divergence: fraction of speculative-token windows where authoritative tokens differ from speculative tokens (target: <= 6% for model-speculate; <= 1% for soft-speculate).\\n  - Commit rate: percentage of speculative windows that are committed vs aborted (target: >= 90% for soft-speculate; >= 70% for model-speculate).\\n  - Quality delta: A/B evals on downstream quality signals (e.g., Rouge/BLEU/LLM-specific evals on prompt sets). No statistically significant drop vs baseline (alpha=0.01).\\n  - Latency improvements: median client-perceived time-to-first-meaningful-token (TTFMT) should improve by >= 8% for spec-enabled traffic.\\n  - Resource overhead: additional GPU/VRAM utilization attributable to speculation <= 10% of baseline capacity at canary scale.\\n  - Error surface: speculative-specific errors (overlay evictions, preempted specs) must be < 0.1% of requests.\\n- Safety gates (automatic):\\n  - If token-level divergence > 10% over 1h, immediate rollback of speculation path for that model.\\n  - If commit rate < configured minimum for 30m (rolling), disable speculation for the model variant.\\n  - If P99 latency for non-spec traffic increases by > 5% absolute, preempt all speculation in impacted region/instance.\\n\\nRollback and canary isolation details:\\n- Rollback granularity: model_variant, region, pool, route. Can roll back speculation codepath for a model without removing the model entirely (configurable).\\n- Automated rollback flow:\\n  1) Detection triggers via metrics alerting rules.\\n  2) Orchestration layer marks the model variant/speculation flag as disabled and pushes policy to router/scheduler.\\n  3) Instances gracefully cancel speculative in-flight tasks (finish current token then abort speculative continuation) and invalidate overlays.\\n  4) Telemetry events emitted: speculation.rollback.triggered, speculation.rollback.completed, speculation.rollback.reason.\\n- Human-in-the-loop: we add a manual-confirm rollback for anything that affects >5% of traffic; automatic rollback for small canaries is allowed.\\n\\nObservability and telemetry (instrumentation plan):\\n- Core events (per-request dimensioned):\\n  - speculation.request.start {speculation_id, model_variant, mode, route, route_tier}\\n  - speculation.run.complete {speculation_id, outcome: committed|aborted|preempted|evicted, commit_latency_ms}\\n  - speculation.confidence.summary {entropy, max_logit_margin}\\n  - kv.overlay.merge {speculation_id, keys_merged}\\n  - speculation.rollback.{triggered|completed}\\n- Metrics to be derived:\\n  - speculation.commit_rate (per-model, per-route)\\n  - speculation.divergence_rate (per-model)\\n  - speculation.latency_benefit.p50/p95/p99 (client perceived)\\n  - speculation.cpu_gpu_overhead_pct (per-node)\\n- Dashboards and alerts:\\n  - Canary dashboard showing divergence vs quality evals, commit rate, and resource overhead.\\n  - SLO alerts: speculative_preemption_rate > threshold, divergence spikes, commit_rate drop.\\n\\nExample request flow (simplified):\\n1) Request arrives, route config indicates speculation allowed and selects mode=soft-speculate.\\n2) Scheduler checks headroom, admits speculative job into low-prio queue and allocates a quantized kernel slot.\\n3) Spec kernel runs and writes overlay entries for KV keys and emits speculation.request.start. Client receives tentative tokens with speculation markers.\\n4) Primary model kernel begins; reads committed cache + overlays. It produces authoritative tokens.\\n5) Primary kernel compares the token window with speculative output; if identical: overlay is committed; telemetry emits speculation.run.complete outcome=committed and overlay merge. If not identical: outcome=aborted and speculative tokens are replaced client-side where protocol allows, or authoritative tokens are appended with correction metadata.\\n\\nTesting and validation plan:\\n- Unit tests for overlay merge/abort semantics and eviction behavior.\\n- Integration tests simulating concurrent spec and authoritative runs with simulated preemption and cache eviction.\\n- Load tests at 0.5%, 5%, and 20% speculation intensity measuring latency tail and memory pressure.\\n- Golden prompt set: curated set of production prompts for automated divergence and quality checks.\\n\\nOpen questions / decisions needed:\\n- UI behavior: what is the default client experience when speculative tokens are later aborted? (options: visual rollback, replace text, show correction markers).\\n- Billing model: do we bill speculative tokens? If yes, at what discount? Need product/finance input.\\n- How to define per-route headroom safely for mixed-traffic environments? Propose starting conservative and exposing a route knob to opt into higher speculation caps.\\n- Kernel contract: how detailed should the confidence summary be for effective commit heuristics? (more telemetry increases overhead).\\n\\nAppendix: proposed rollout timeline (high level)\\n- Week 0-2: implement kernel and KV overlay primitives + unit tests.\\n- Week 3-4: local integration, overlay merging, and synthetic load tests.\\n- Week 5: internal dogfood on dev cluster with opt-in routes.\\n- Week 6-8: 0.5% canary for model variants + dashboards and alerts.\\n- Week 9-12: expand canary to 5% and run extended quality evals; iterate on acceptance thresholds.\\n\\nAction items:\\n- Product: confirm billing stance for speculative tokens (assigned: Mariana).\\n- Platform/SRE: define safe default headroom calculation and add scheduler admission control hooks (assigned: Evan).\\n- Serving runtime: prototype overlay KV API and speculative annotations in kernel interface (assigned: Daniel).\\n\\nIf we want, I can break this into a narrower PRD focusing only on KV overlay APIs or only on the scheduler admission control. For now this is intended as a cross-team working draft to iterate against concrete impl PRs.\\n\\nEnd of document.",
  "title_field_name": "title",
  "content_field_names": [
    "content"
  ],
  "dataset_doc_uuid": "dsid_cf59c9d7c95d4cd184713088627f2e37"
}
